provenance.other: “Bread to the hungry” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Isaiah 58:7 and Ezekiel 18:7 and 18:16 — and 'covered the naked' in exactly two, both of them Ezekiel 18. 'Hath oppressed the poor' is a KJV singleton at Ezekiel 18:12. The Book of Mormon's three items ('oppression to the poor, withholding their food from the hungry, withholding their clothing from the naked') reproduce Ezekiel's three in Ezekiel's order. Ezekiel 18:16 also supplies the verb: 'hath not withholden the pledge'.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 18 is the KJV's set-piece on whether a generation inherits its fathers' guilt, and it works by two parallel catalogues — what the just man does (18:5-9) and what his wicked son does (18:10-13) — each item of the second answering an item of the first. Helaman 4:12 is that catalogue run once more in a third form: not a list of deeds but a list of gerunds, and not the wicked son's positive crimes but the just man's virtues negated. Feeding the hungry becomes 'withholding their food from the hungry'; covering the naked becomes 'withholding their clothing from the naked'; not oppressing becomes 'oppression to the poor'. Recover Ezekiel and the point of the chapter comes with it, which is exactly the point Mormon is making at 4:11-13 — that the great slaughter 'would not have happened, had it not been for their wickedness'. Ezekiel 18 is the chapter that insists the soul that sinneth, it shall die, and that a people's disaster is its own doing; Mormon has quietly borrowed the KJV's own argument for national desert.

4:12.note: 'Their oppression to the poor, withholding their food from the hungry, withholding their clothing from the naked.' Three items, three KJV rarities, one chapter. Ezekiel 18's catalogue of the righteous man is here inverted item by item, and the inversion is the argument: what Mormon lists is not a set of crimes but a set of omissions, which is how Ezekiel 18 defines wickedness in the first place. Isaiah 58:7 is the other home of 'bread to the hungry' and is likely fused in — Isaiah 58 is the fast that God chooses, and the naked there are covered too — but Ezekiel supplies the oppression, the withholding, and the sequence.
4:12.text: And hath not oppressed any, but hath restored to the debtor his pledge, hath spoiled none by violence, hath given his bread to the hungry, and hath covered the naked with a garment;

provenance.other: “committing adultery” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the longer run “stealing, and committing adultery” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Committing adultery' is a KJV singleton at Hosea 4:2, and so is the longer run 'stealing, and committing adultery'. The 1830 spells it 'steeling'; 1920 normalizes to 'stealing'. Jeremiah 7:9's decalogue-list ('Will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery') is the only near competitor and uses finite verbs, not participles.
provenance.significance: Hosea 4:2 is the prophet's indictment of a land in which 'there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God', and its next clause is 'they break out, and blood toucheth blood' — which is the chapter's own subject at 4:1, 'insomuch that there was much bloodshed'. What makes the borrowing pointed is Hosea 4:6: 'my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge'. Mormon's verse is the inventory of a nation whose destruction he has just said was self-inflicted, written in the participial form the KJV uses at exactly one place, and that place explains the bloodshed by the sin-list rather than by the enemy.

4:12.note: 'Murdering, plundering, lying, steeling, committing adultery.' The KJV has one verse that strings sins together as participles and it is Hosea 4:2, whose own string is 'swearing, and lying, and killing, and stealing, and committing adultery'. Three of the Book of Mormon's five are Hosea's three in Hosea's order, and 'committing adultery' occurs nowhere else in the KJV. That the list is built out of the KJV's one participial sin-catalogue is a stronger fact about it than any single word.
4:12.text: By swearing, and lying, and killing, and stealing, and committing adultery, they break out, and blood toucheth blood.

provenance.other: “Make a mock” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Adjudicated at Jacob 6:8, where the object of the mockery is the plan of redemption; the argument is made there and is not restated.
provenance.significance: Proverbs 14:9's mocker is a fool and his object is sin. Jacob 6:8 redirected the idiom at the remedy; Helaman 4:12 redirects it at 'that which was sacred', which is nearer Proverbs' own register and pairs, four clauses later in this chapter, with Matthew 7:6's 'that which is holy' at 4:22. Read with that link, the two verses divide Matthew's sentence between them: the holy thing mocked here, trampled underfoot there.

4:12.note: 'Making a mock of that which was sacred.' The phrase is a KJV singleton and the link is written rather than filed as a recurrence because Helaman is a new book in a new hand (ADJUDICATING §4). The argument was made at Jacob 6:8; what is new here is the object, 'that which was sacred', which stands in the same relation to Matthew 7:6's 'that which is holy' as 4:22's trampling does to Matthew's.
4:12.whyNot: Three words, and 'make a mock of' had independent currency in nineteenth-century English; the phrase could arrive without Proverbs.
4:12.text: Fools make a mock at sin: but among the righteous there is favour.

provenance.route: Micah 5:1 (with Job 16:10 and 2 Chronicles 18:23) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Upon the cheek” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: 2 Chronicles 18:23 (Zedekiah smites Micaiah), Job 16:10 ('they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully'), Psalm 3:7 ('the cheek bone'), and Micah 5:1. No one of the four can be isolated on wording alone.
provenance.significance: What the four verses have in common is the point. In the KJV nobody is ever struck on the cheek except a prophet, a righteous sufferer, or a judge — Micaiah by the court prophet, Job by his mockers, the judge of Israel by the besieger. The gesture is the KJV's emblem of contempt shown to the person who is in the right. Helaman 4:12 gives it to 'their humble brethren', in a chapter whose every date is counted by 'the reign of the Judges', and Micah 5:1 is the KJV's one verse where a judge is smitten on the cheek. That coincidence is not an argument for Micah as the source; it is what the borrowing does once made. The New Testament's 'whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek' (Matthew 5:39) is a different idiom — 'on', not 'upon' — and is not in view.

4:12.note: 'And smiting their humble brethren upon the cheek.' Proposed under the generative posture (CONVENTIONS §0a). The prepositional phrase is a four-verse KJV rarity with a consistent sense, and the Book of Mormon uses it in that sense: the humiliation of the righteous by those with power over them. Micah 5:1 is named as source because it is the only one in which the person struck holds an office, which is the office this book dates itself by; the other three are recorded as composite rather than excluded, because the wording does not choose between them.
4:12.whyNot: Four words and one preposition, spread across four possible sources with no verbal test to separate them. If the borrowing is from Job 16:10 the judge reading disappears entirely, and nothing else in Helaman 4 touches Micah.
4:12.text: Now gather thyself in troops, O daughter of troops: he hath laid siege against us: they shall smite the judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek.

provenance.other: “The spirit of prophecy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. This is its first occurrence in Helaman; the phrase returns eleven verses later at 4:23, where it is paired with 'the spirit of revelation' again.
provenance.significance: Revelation 19:10 defines the phrase as it gives it: 'the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.' Helaman 4:12 lists 'denying the spirit of prophecy and of revelation' among the sins that lost the land, which — with Revelation's gloss recovered — makes the sin a denial of the testimony of Jesus, not merely of an office. The catalogue this sits in is otherwise Ezekiel's and Hosea's, all of it social and none of it christological; the one New Testament item in the list is the one that names what is being refused.

4:12.note: A KJV singleton, adjudicated repeatedly from Jacob 1:6 onward and written here because Helaman is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4). Recorded at first use in the book; 4:23's repetition is Mormon reusing his own clause and is registered as a recurrence rather than a second link.
4:12.text: And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

provenance.other: 'Boastings' — the plural noun — occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The singular 'boasting' is commoner (Romans 3:27, 2 Corinthians 7:14 and others), which is what makes the plural worth counting.
provenance.significance: James 4:16 sits inside the KJV's most sustained attack on self-reliance: 'God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble' (4:6), then the merchant who says he will go into such a city and buy and sell and get gain, who does not know what shall be on the morrow, and whose confidence James answers with 'ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil'. Helaman 4:12-13 has run the same sequence in the same order — pride of heart, exceeding riches, contempt for the humble brethren, and then 'their boastings in their own strength'. The sentence that follows is the KJV's verdict carried out: 'they were left in their own strength'.

4:13.note: 'And their boastings in their own strength, they were left in their own strength.' One word, but a KJV singleton in the plural, arriving at the end of a paragraph that has already worked through James 4's own sequence of pride, riches and the humble. The epigram Mormon builds around it — boasted in their own strength, therefore left in it — is his own and is in no version of the Bible; what is borrowed is the noun and the frame it comes in.
4:13.whyNot: A single word, and 'boastings' is ordinary nineteenth-century English requiring no KJV source at all. The James context is suggestive but no clause is shared, and nothing else in the chapter touches the epistle.
4:13.text: But now ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil.

provenance.other: “set at nought” occurs in exactly five KJV verses and “stiffnecked people” occurs in exactly six KJV verses. 'Set at nought' occurs in five KJV verses: Proverbs 1:25, Mark 9:12, Acts 4:11, Acts 19:27 and Romans 14:10. Only Proverbs has divine instruction as the object; the four New Testament occurrences all have a person or a trade set at nought. 'Stiffnecked people' occurs in six, all of them Exodus 32-34 or Deuteronomy 9. The 1830 spells it 'nought'; 1920 modernizes to 'naught', which moves the word away from the KJV's spelling (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: Proverbs 1:24-31 is the KJV's one passage in which wisdom, having been set at nought, refuses to answer when the disaster arrives: 'Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer.' Helaman 4:21 is the verse in which the Nephites, with the Lamanites in Zarahemla, 'began to remember the prophecies of Alma, and also the words of Mosiah' — remembering, that is, precisely the counsel they had set at nought, at precisely the point in Proverbs' sequence where remembering is too late. The chapter then follows Proverbs' outcome to the letter at 4:25: 'they must unavoidably perish.'

4:21.note: 'They had been a stiffnecked people, and that they had set at nought the commandments of God.' Two KJV formulas in one clause, and the second is doing more work than its count suggests: of the five verses containing 'set at nought', only Proverbs 1:25 has instruction from God as what is set at nought, and the Proverbs passage is about the moment of belated remembering that this verse describes. The 'stiffnecked people' half is the Exodus 32/Deuteronomy 9 formula and carries no single source; it is recorded as composite rather than argued.
4:21.whyNot: Three common words. The phrase is available from any of five KJV verses and from ordinary English, and the argument rests on the fit of Proverbs 1's scenario rather than on the wording.
4:21.text: But ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof:

provenance.other: “under their feet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “trample” occurs in exactly three KJV verses. 'Under their feet' is a KJV singleton at Matthew 7:6, and 'trample' occurs in only three KJV verses (Psalm 91:13 'under feet', Isaiah 63:3, Matthew 7:6). Helaman 4:22 has both halves of the singleton: 'trampled under their feet'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 7:6 is about entrusting a holy thing to keepers who will not keep it, and its verbs come in that order: give not that which is holy, lest they trample it under their feet, and turn again and rend you. Helaman 4 distributes the sentence across two verses. At 4:12 the people are 'making a mock of that which was sacred'; at 4:22 they have 'trampled under their feet the laws of Mosiah, or that which the Lord commanded him to give unto the people' — and the relative clause names the giving that Matthew forbids. Then the rending: 'they had become weak … driven before the Lamanites.' What the laws of Mosiah are being called, by the borrowing, is the pearl.

4:22.note: Four words of a KJV singleton, with the pronoun Matthew has. This is the same phrase adjudicated at 1 Nephi 19:7 and Alma 60:33 and it is written again here because Helaman is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4) and because the object is new: not the words of the prophets and not the laws of God in general, but a named legal code, given by a named lawgiver, at the moment the book stops being able to date itself by that code. Read with 4:12's 'that which was sacred', the two verses hold the two halves of Matthew's sentence.
4:22.text: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.

provenance.other: “Dwelleth in you” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 8:11 and 1 Corinthians 3:16, and only 1 Corinthians has the temple. 'Unholy' occurs in four KJV verses and never of a building; the adjective is the Book of Mormon's own back-formation from 1 Corinthians 3:17's 'the temple of God is holy'. The n-gram stream ranked 1 Corinthians 3:16 in this verse on 'and that the spirit of'.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a question with a threat under it — 'Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you? If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are.' Helaman 4:24 states the same doctrine as a general maxim and then uses it to explain a military defeat: the Spirit withdrew because the temple was defiled, and 'therefore the Lord did cease to preserve them'. Paul's 'him shall God destroy' is not quoted, but it is what the chapter has spent twenty-three verses describing, and the plural 'temples' converts Paul's congregational image into a statement about individual bodies — which is 1 Corinthians 6:19's move, made with 3:16's vocabulary.

4:24.note: 'Because the spirit of the Lord doth not dwell in unholy temples.' A maxim built from Paul's question, with the affirmation negated and the adjective inverted: the Spirit dwells in you, the temple of God is holy, therefore the Spirit does not dwell in unholy temples. The KJV never calls a temple unholy; the word exists in it only of persons (1 Timothy 1:9, 2 Timothy 3:2), which is exactly the sense the plural requires here.
4:24.text: Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?

provenance.other: “Become weak” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Judges 16:17 and Isaiah 14:10. But the proximate model here is not the KJV: Mosiah 1:13 reads 'that thereby they become weak, like unto their brethren; and he will no more preserve them, by his matchless and marvellous power', and Helaman 4:24-25 reads 'they had become weak, like unto their brethren, the Lamanites, and that the spirit of the Lord did no more preserve them … therefore the Lord did cease to preserve them by his miraculous and matchless power'. 'Matchless' occurs in no KJV verse at all; it is Benjamin's word, and its reappearance is what fixes the route.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 14:10 — 'Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us?' — has both 'become weak' and 'become like unto', and is thematically apt for a chapter about pride brought low. It is not preferred, because it cannot account for 'preserve' or for 'matchless'.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's conditional at Mosiah 1:13 was Samson's, transposed to a nation: a people set apart, strong only by a kept condition, one transgression away from being indistinguishable from their brethren, with Judges 16:20's 'he wist not that the LORD was departed from him' behind 'he will no more preserve them'. Helaman 4 is that conditional discharged. What Benjamin said would happen has happened, in his words, and Mormon marks it by keeping the one word in the sentence that belongs to no Bible — 'matchless'. The metalepsis therefore runs through two texts, not one: recover Mosiah 1 and the defeat is the fulfilment of a warning; recover Judges behind Mosiah and the nation is Samson waking to find his strength gone.

4:24.note: This is the clearest OT-via-earlier-BoM case in the chapter and the mediation field carries the finding. The Samson argument was made at Mosiah 1:13 and is not restated; what is claimed here is that Helaman 4:24-25 quotes Benjamin rather than Judges. Three things establish it: 'become weak, like unto their brethren' reproduces Benjamin's clause including the 'brethren' that stands where Judges has 'any other man'; 'did no more preserve them' reproduces his verb; and 'matchless power', in the very next verse, reproduces a word that occurs nowhere in the KJV. Mormon has taken a hundred-and-thirty-year-old royal warning and used it as the caption for a military collapse.
4:24.text: That he told her all his heart, and said unto her, There hath not come a razor upon mine head; for I have been a Nazarite unto God from my mother’s womb: if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me, and I shall become weak, and be like any other man.

provenance.other: “cleave unto the LORD” occurs in exactly three KJV verses. 'Cleave unto the LORD' occurs in three KJV verses: Deuteronomy 4:4, Joshua 23:8 and Acts 11:23. The first two add 'your God', which the Book of Mormon has as 'their God'. Joshua 23:8 is the imperative form; Deuteronomy 4:4 is the descriptive.
provenance.significance: Joshua 23 is the farewell speech in which Joshua tells Israel that the nations left in the land are left there deliberately, and that if they do not cleave unto the LORD those nations 'shall be snares and traps unto you … until ye perish from off this good land'. Helaman 4:25 reaches the identical conclusion in the identical order: the Lamanites are more numerous, the Nephites hold half their lands, and 'except they should cleave unto the Lord their God, they must unavoidably perish'. Joshua 23:13's 'until ye perish' is the clause Mormon's 'must unavoidably perish' answers to, and the situation — a remnant of the land held, a stronger population beside them — is Joshua 23's exactly.

4:25.note: 'And except they should cleave unto the Lord their God, they must unavoidably perish.' Three words, available from three KJV verses, but the conditional they sit in belongs to one of them: Joshua 23 is the KJV's one passage that makes cleaving unto the LORD the condition of not perishing before the nations left in the land. That is the chapter's own military situation, described three verses earlier.
4:25.whyNot: Deuteronomy 4:4 has the same three words and the same 'your God', and 'cleave unto' is a common enough covenant idiom that the choice between the two rests on context alone.
4:25.text: But cleave unto the LORD your God, as ye have done unto this day.
